items.readable_text:
Content:
Let [MATH: V] be a vector space. Any function [MATH: f:V \times V \to \mathbb{R}] that takes two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in V] and returns a real number is an inner product on [MATH: V,] denoted [MATH: \langle \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b} \rangle,] if the following axioms are satisfied:

Content:
- Linearity in the first argument:
[MATH: ⟨a + b, c⟩ = ⟨a, c⟩ + ⟨b, c⟩; ⟨αa, b⟩ = α⟨a, b⟩, α ∈ R]
- Symmetry:
[MATH: \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle]
- Positive definiteness:
[MATH: \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle \gt 0\quad \textrm{for}\quad \mathbf a\neq \mathbf 0]
[MATH: \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0\quad \Leftrightarrow\quad \mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}]

Content:
The concept of an inner product is a generalization of the dot product. It allows us to apply the geometric ideas of length and angle to abstract vector spaces.

Content:
Notice that the standard dot product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] indeed satisfies these axioms. Recall that if [MATH: \mathbf u, \mathbf v \in \mathbb R^n,] then
[MATH: \langle \mathbf u, \mathbf v\rangle = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = u_1\cdot v_1 + u_2\cdot v_2 + \cdots + u_n\cdot v_n .]
Let [MATH: \mathbf u, \mathbf v, \mathbf w \in\mathbb R^n] and [MATH: \alpha \in \mathbb R.] Let's now check that our three axioms are satisfied.

Content:
- We first show that the dot product is linear in the first argument.
[MATH: ⟨u + v, w⟩|= (u + v) ⋅ w; = u ⋅ w + v ⋅ w; = ⟨u, w⟩ + ⟨v, w⟩✓; ⟨αu, v⟩|= (αu) ⋅ v; = (αu ⋅ v); = α(u ⋅ v); = α⟨u, v⟩✓]
- Next, we show that the dot product is symmetric:
[MATH: ⟨u, v⟩|= u ⋅ v; = v ⋅ u; = ⟨v, u⟩✓]
- Finally, we show that the dot product is positive definite:
[MATH: ⟨u, u⟩|= u ⋅ u; = u_{1}u_{1} + u_{2}u_{2} + ⋯ + u_{n}u_{n}; = u_{1}^{2} + u_{2}^{2} + ⋯ + u_{n}^{2},]
which is clearly positive for all [MATH: \mathbf u\neq\mathbf 0] and is zero for [MATH: \mathbf u = \mathbf 0 \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

Content:
Since the dot product satisfies our three axioms, we conclude that it is an inner product.

Content:
Finally, note that since an inner product is both linear in the first argument and symmetric, then it is also linear in the second argument.

Content:
The next inner product that we will discuss concerns inner products on polynomials.

Content:
Given a sequence of distinct real numbers [MATH: t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_{n+1},] the function
[MATH: \langle x(t), y(t) \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^{n+1} x(t_i) y(t_i)]
defines an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}_n[t],] the vector space of polynomials of degree at most [MATH: n.]

Content:
Let's consider a few examples:

Content:
- The following function defines an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}_1[t]\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)]

Content:
- The following function defines an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}_2[t]\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)]
- The following function defines an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}_3[t]\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1) + p(2)q(2)]

Content:
Notice that this inner product on [MATH: \mathbb R_n[t]] requires summing [MATH: n+1] terms. This is essential to ensure positive definiteness. For example, the function
[MATH: \langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)]
is not an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb R_3[t],] since there exist nonzero polynomials [MATH: f(x)\in\mathbb R_3[t]] such that [MATH: f(-1) = f(0) = f(1) = 0,] which violates the condition [MATH: \langle f(x), f(x) \rangle > 0.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let [MATH: V] be a vector space. Any function [MATH: f:V \times V \to \mathbb{R}] that takes two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in V] and returns a real number is an inner product on [MATH: V,] denoted [MATH: \langle \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b} \rangle,] if the following axioms are satisfied:

Content:
- Linearity in the first argument:
[MATH: ⟨a + b, c⟩ = ⟨a, c⟩ + ⟨b, c⟩; ⟨αa, b⟩ = α⟨a, b⟩, α ∈ R]
- Symmetry:
[MATH: \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a} \rangle]
- Positive definiteness:
[MATH: \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle \gt 0\quad \textrm{for}\quad \mathbf a\neq \mathbf 0]
[MATH: \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle = 0\quad \Leftrightarrow\quad \mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}]

Content:
The concept of an inner product is a generalization of the dot product. It allows us to apply the geometric ideas of length and angle to abstract vector spaces.

Content:
Notice that the standard dot product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] indeed satisfies these axioms. Recall that if [MATH: \mathbf u, \mathbf v \in \mathbb R^n,] then
[MATH: \langle \mathbf u, \mathbf v\rangle = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = u_1\cdot v_1 + u_2\cdot v_2 + \cdots + u_n\cdot v_n .]
Let [MATH: \mathbf u, \mathbf v, \mathbf w \in\mathbb R^n] and [MATH: \alpha \in \mathbb R.] Let's now check that our three axioms are satisfied.

Content:
- We first show that the dot product is linear in the first argument.
[MATH: ⟨u + v, w⟩|= (u + v) ⋅ w; = u ⋅ w + v ⋅ w; = ⟨u, w⟩ + ⟨v, w⟩✓; ⟨αu, v⟩|= (αu) ⋅ v; = (αu ⋅ v); = α(u ⋅ v); = α⟨u, v⟩✓]
- Next, we show that the dot product is symmetric:
[MATH: ⟨u, v⟩|= u ⋅ v; = v ⋅ u; = ⟨v, u⟩✓]
- Finally, we show that the dot product is positive definite:
[MATH: ⟨u, u⟩|= u ⋅ u; = u_{1}u_{1} + u_{2}u_{2} + ⋯ + u_{n}u_{n}; = u_{1}^{2} + u_{2}^{2} + ⋯ + u_{n}^{2},]
which is clearly positive for all [MATH: \mathbf u\neq\mathbf 0] and is zero for [MATH: \mathbf u = \mathbf 0 \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

Content:
Since the dot product satisfies our three axioms, we conclude that it is an inner product.

Content:
Finally, note that since an inner product is both linear in the first argument and symmetric, then it is also linear in the second argument.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Weighted Dot Product

Content:
The first type of inner product that we will discuss is the weighted dot product.

Content:
Given a sequence of positive real numbers [MATH: d_1, d_2, \ldots d_n > 0,] called "weights", the function
[MATH: \langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^n d_i x_i y_i]
defines an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.] This is similar to the dot product, except here, different components are given different weights.

---

[MATH: [1; − 2; 0]]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Computing the inner product according to the definition, we get

[MATH: ⟨x, y⟩|= 3x_{1}y_{1} + x_{2}y_{2} + 7x_{3}y_{3}; = 3 ⋅ 1 ⋅ (− 3) + (− 2) ⋅ 1 + 7 ⋅ 0 ⋅ 5; = − 9 − 2 + 0; = − 11.]

Item 6 — Tutorial: An Inner Product of Polynomials in One Variable

Content:
The next inner product that we will discuss concerns inner products on polynomials.

Content:
Given a sequence of distinct real numbers [MATH: t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_{n+1},] the function
[MATH: \langle x(t), y(t) \rangle = \sum_{i=1}^{n+1} x(t_i) y(t_i)]
defines an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}_n[t],] the vector space of polynomials of degree at most [MATH: n.]

Content:
Let's consider a few examples:

Content:
- The following function defines an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}_1[t]\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)]

Content:
- The following function defines an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}_2[t]\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)]
- The following function defines an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb{R}_3[t]\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: \langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1) + p(2)q(2)]

Content:
Notice that this inner product on [MATH: \mathbb R_n[t]] requires summing [MATH: n+1] terms. This is essential to ensure positive definiteness. For example, the function
[MATH: \langle p(x), q(x)\rangle = p(-1)q(-1) + p(0)q(0) + p(1)q(1)]
is not an inner product on [MATH: \mathbb R_3[t],] since there exist nonzero polynomials [MATH: f(x)\in\mathbb R_3[t]] such that [MATH: f(-1) = f(0) = f(1) = 0,] which violates the condition [MATH: \langle f(x), f(x) \rangle > 0.]

---

Item 10 — Tutorial: An Inner Product of Functions in One Variable

Content:
Our final inner product is a generalization of what we saw in the previous example. The function
[MATH: \langle x(t), y(t) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} x(t) y(t) \, \textrm{d}t]
defines an inner product on [MATH: \mathcal{C}[a,b],] the vector space of continuous functions on [MATH: [a,b].]

Content:
Here, instead of finding the product of the functions at some discrete points and summing them, we sum (integrate) the product of the functions over the whole interval [MATH: [a,b].]
